claims.text: The tribo-corrosion response is governed by competition between mechanical removal of the passive oxide film and its localized re-formation.
Film removal and re-formation produce heterogeneous surface conditions.
Heterogeneous surface conditions promote localized corrosion within wear tracks.
Localized corrosion at wear tracks accelerates material degradation.
The proposed initial alloy is equiatomic and has a fine, multiphase microstructure.
The proposed initial alloy has a naturally formed, uniform passive oxide film.
Mechanical sliding disrupts the protective oxide layer and exposes fresh metal to the corrosive environment.
Rapid localized re-passivation creates spatially heterogeneous electrochemical potentials.
Spatially heterogeneous potentials enhance localized galvanic activity.
Wear intensifies corrosion under the proposed tribo-corrosion conditions.
Combined tribo-corrosion will produce greater total degradation than the isolated wear and static-corrosion baselines.
Wear-track depth under combined tribo-corrosion will be greater than under isolated wear.
Corrosion-pit density and size under combined tribo-corrosion will be greater than under static corrosion.
In the isolated dry-wear and static-corrosion baselines, the passive film remains largely intact and the degradation mechanisms do not interact synergistically.
The proposed mechanism should operate when film removal is as fast as or faster than film re-formation.
The mechanism should fail or change when sliding is too mild to disrupt the passive film.
The mechanism should fail or change when aggressive corrosion uniformly degrades the passive layer and eliminates localized galvanic effects.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says mechanical wear disrupts the protective oxide, whereas the baseline broadly states that the passive film remains largely intact in isolated dry wear as well as static corrosion.
The nominal wear baseline is inconsistently described as dry wear, wear in an inert environment, and wear in an inert fluid; these are not necessarily equivalent controls.

The prediction only requires combined degradation to exceed the matched individual baselines, while the falsification rule requires it to exceed the sum of isolated wear and corrosion. A result could therefore satisfy the stated prediction yet be classified as falsifying the hypothesis.
